items.title: Power Grids on 5 Continents Pulse Every 60 Seconds. Scientists Think They Finally Know Why.
items.summary: There are many things about modern life we take for granted – perhaps none more so than the vast electrical grids that power so much of it. But for many years, these grids have been doing something strange. Every 60 seconds, they pulse – a tiny change in the frequency that subsides only to recur 60 seconds later. And it's not just one power grid. Around the world, multiple power grids – physically isolated from each other – have been found doing the same thing. It's precise, and it has persisted, year after year, for more than a decade. This precision suggests that it's not an accident, but it has remained a curiously enduring puzzle. Now, scientists think they have found the answer – and it's surprisingly mundane. Every minute, some uninterruptible power supplies – the backup systems used in places like hospitals, data centers, and research facilities – perform routine battery checks, creating small but measurable surges in electricity demand. And it's like clockwork. "Even benign control routines can become systemically relevant when many devices act coherently," writes a team led by physicist Dirk Witthaut of the University of Cologne, Germany, in a paper published in Nature Energy.

items.title: The global socket: how threat actors are weaponizing GSocket for stealthy C2
items.summary: Microsoft observed multiple incidents in which threat actors deployed GSocket, an open source remote access tool, on compromised Linux servers. Threat actors used Gsocket to maintain access even after the vulnerabilities used for initial compromise were remediated. This turned a single web application compromise into persistent access that outlasted the remediation of the original vulnerabilities. Defenders investigating affected hosts should look for evidence of GSocket deployment, persistence, privilege escalation, and outbound connections, rather than treating application patching alone as complete remediation. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows this activity growing over recent months and concentrated on web applications and hosting environments. GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. The same relay model that supports legitimate remote administration also gives threat actors a way to maintain access without operating dedicated C2 infrastructure. Once GSocket runs on a compromised server, the server and the operator each connect outbound to the Global Socket Relay Network, which pairs the two sessions over an end-to-end encrypted channel. Because GSocket runs independently of the exploited application, patching the vulnerability does not remove the relay client or its persistence. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows that this activity is not limited to a single compromise. From March through August 2026, devices with GSocket-related detections increased 356.2%, although the increase was not consistent month to month.

items.title: How AI Revived a Stalled Attack on a U.S. Retailer
items.summary: In September 2026, attackers broke into a U.S. retail organization but struggled to progress the intrusion. Overnight their pattern of activity changed, and it was clear that they began using an AI to assist them and find a way around the obstacles thrown in their path. None of the techniques used in this second phase of the attack were new. What changed was how quickly the attackers identified a complex workaround and how reliably it was applied. About 10 minutes after first querying the SolarWinds Orion service on the victim’s server, they had identified an unfamiliar message broker, taken its shared secret and used it to reach another host. Some of the scripts used carried comments that appear to record a model's reasoning, and the timing between commands points to a human operator relaying output to an AI tool rather than an autonomous agent. The primary victim was a U.S. retail organization. The attackers worked across its internet-facing web server and at least six further servers, most of which ran Microsoft SQL Server. They searched point-of-sale synchronization scripts for stored passwords, which may indicate a focus on retail systems. Symantec also found overlaps in loader files and infrastructure with an August 2026 intrusion at a different organization and a July 2026 intrusion at a securities firm. Neither showed signs of AI assistance. The staging server used in August was the same one used against the retailer, and a reverse proxy tool known as Yuze also appeared on a host at that organization.

items.title: Attackers Use Autonomous AI to Target Semiconductor, Defense and Civil Society Sectors
items.summary: From August–September 2026, Chinese-speaking attackers used an open-source AI penetration testing framework called Cairn to autonomously conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. The attackers weaponized Cairn by pairing it with Chinese AI models Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek. The attackers supplied a target and a goal, then Cairn planned, executed and recorded results on its own. These attacks achieved unauthorized access or data retrieval at 10 of the targeted organizations, including: * Accessing dozens of valid credentials * Mass exposing personal data (exceeding one million records at one organization) * Retrieving military and government identities * Creating persistent administrator accounts in a production system * Modifying a live industry standards-ballot document We assess with moderate confidence that this activity represents China-nexus intelligence collection, which we currently track as CL-STA-1238. This article details how attackers used Cairn to target three key sectors: * Advanced semiconductor manufacturing * U.S. defense policy * Civil society

items.title: Following additional security disclosures, N-able is taking further precautionary action to protect N-central customers.
items.summary: Classification: Critical, Solution: Workaround, Exploit Maturity: Proof-of-Concept, CVSSv3.1: None, CVEs: , Summary: Following additional security disclosures, N-able is taking further precautionary action to protect N-central customers. As the situation continues to evolve, we will share any further updates and guidance here. We are restricting certain N-central features and integrations. These measures may affect some functionality, but we believe taking additional precautions while remediation is completed is the right action to protect our partners and their customers. N-central HOSTED Customers: N-able has applied these temporary protections directly to Hosted environments. No server-side action is required from Hosted customers. * Legacy API is turned off by default in the product. * Intune integration has been turned off while additional protections are implemented and validated. This is a precautionary step. * Hosted customers should continue to follow our previous guidance to upgrade Agents and Probes. N-central ON-PREMISES Customers: Ensure Legacy API access is disabled in your environment. * Legacy API access is disabled by default. If you enabled it, follow these instructions: How to Disable Legacy API settings on On-Premises N-central servers * As a precaution, if you are running the Intune integration, we have temporarily deactivated it for you. If we were unable to execute this, our support team will make contact with you. This is a precautionary step. * On-Premises customers should also continue to follow the previously communicated HF2 guidance, including upgrading their Agents and Probes See also: https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/new-n-central-exploits-work-against.html, See also: https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-n-able-4everable2shell-zero-day-exploited-hours-after-poc-released/

items.title: PHP2Shell Exploitation on Check Point Gateway
items.summary: We have now confirmed that, in late October 2026, approximately one week after a security fix became available, activity originating from 130.94.19[.]204 targeted Israeli organizations through vulnerable Mobile Access portals on Check Point Security Gateways. Evidence suggested some cases of a successful compromise, with exploitation activity consistent with PHP2Shell, associated with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Following initial access, the attacker escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by exploiting CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege-escalation vulnerability in the DynamicCLI IPC interface. The attacker then used privileged command execution to deploy PHP webshells and establish persistence. A second scanning wave on November 2nd targeted some Israeli organizations previously targeted during the first wave, alongside additional organizations worldwide, with no apparent focus on Israel. Neither wave showed a clear sector preference, suggesting opportunistic initial-access attempts rather than sector-specific targeting.

items.title: Critical Red Hat Quay Flaw Lets Attackers Read and Overwrite All Private Container Images in a Registry
items.summary: Classification: Critical, Solution: Official Fix, Exploit Maturity: Not Defined, CVSSv3.1: 9.9, CVEs: CVE-2026-110697, CVE-2026-123710, Summary: A critical flaw in Red Hat Quay allows an attacker who can access a Quay registry to read and overwrite private container images in every repository. Quay enables anonymous access by default, and while it is enabled, the attacker needs no account. When it is off, anyone with a valid account can still exploit the flaw, Red Hat said yesterday. The company has released fixed builds for eight Quay 3 branches. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-123710 (CVSS score: 9.8). Quay uses keys it trusts to sign the access tokens that allow image pushes and pulls. The flaw lets an attacker add their own key to the keys Quay trusts, with no expiry date. Quay then accepts tokens signed with that key for any repository. With those tokens, an attacker can retrieve private images and any secrets or credentials stored within them. The attacker can also push or overwrite images, and the change propagates to every system that later pulls those images. The planted key survives restarts until someone removes it. It can also be used to delete the keys that running Quay instances use, so normal pushes and pulls start failing with authentication errors. A second critical flaw, CVE-2026-110697 (CVSS score: 9.9), was disclosed at the same time. It lets a Quay user who can create a namespace steal other tenants' robot account tokens and use them to read, push, or overwrite those tenants' images. This flaw is in the code that lists robot accounts. It builds an SQL LIKE pattern from the namespace name without escaping wildcard characters, and in SQL LIKE an underscore matches any single character. So a namespace with an underscore in the right place can match another tenant's namespace and return its robot accounts, with their decrypted tokens. The attacker needs no elevated privileges, and the victim does not have to do anything. See also: https://access.redhat.com/security/cve/cve-2026-110697, See also: https://access.redhat.com/security/cve/cve-2026-123710, See also: https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=2568072, See also: https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7149923

items.title: eBPF Rootkits: Why Underground Actors Are Taking Notice
items.summary: For years, eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) has been one of the most celebrated technologies in the Linux kernel. It lets developers run sandboxed programs inside the kernel without writing kernel modules, while powering everything from network monitoring to security tooling. Linux is extremely popular in production servers and giants like Google, Cloudflare, and Meta rely on it daily. The same eBPF capabilities that are attractive for defenders, however, can be a powerful weapon in the hands of attackers. Flare’s research found underground forum posts sharing eBPF rootkit code and step-by-step tutorials. One Russian-language post described how to build an implant with process hiding and packet-triggered activation, and included screenshots the author presented as demonstrations. An eBPF malware can hook into kernel functions, observe system calls, or inspect and modify network traffic using the same kernel-supported bpf() interface as legitimate tools like Cilium. Its programs run without loading a kernel module, so a routine lsmod check can miss them. The challenge for defenders is determining who loaded the program and what it does.

Its programs run without loading a kernel module, so a routine lsmod check can miss them. The challenge for defenders is determining who loaded the program and what it does.

items.title: Disgraced former CA eMudhra blames buggy script for hopelessly weak certificates
items.summary: Former certification authority eMudhra has claimed a buggy Python script is the main reason it issued laughably insecure digital certificates. The company posted its account of the matter on Bugzilla where a user with the handle “Naveen Kumar ML” wrote “During a single key‑generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, sixteen subordinate (issuing) CA key pairs in eMudhra’s ‘B’ and ‘C’ series were generated correctly on a hardware security module and then processed through an approved wrap/unwrap round‑trip using a custom python key‑handling script.” eMudhra aimed to create eight ECDSA P-384 private keys which should have been 48 bytes long. But the script contained what Kumar described as “a bug/defect in the import code [which] resulted in a read‑back from the unwrapped object that truncated the private value, so the certified public keys correspond to private scalars below the expected range and are recoverable from public information.” The truncation is the key problem here, because it appears that eMudhra ignored 47 of the 48 bytes, producing its infamously insecure single-byte keys such as the number four.

eMudhra aimed to create eight ECDSA P-384 private keys which should have been 48 bytes long. But the script contained what Kumar described as “a bug/defect in the import code [which] resulted in a read‑back from the unwrapped object that truncated the private value, so the certified public keys correspond to private scalars below the expected range and are recoverable from public information.”

The truncation is the key problem here, because it appears that eMudhra ignored 47 of the 48 bytes, producing its infamously insecure single-byte keys such as the number four.

items.title: Microsoft Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 enter their 'permanently vulnerable' era
items.summary: Microsoft has warned customers still clinging to Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 to consider the software "permanently vulnerable" as November's security fixes arrive for Subscription Edition (SE) alone. The warning appears in the release documentation for November's Exchange Server SE security update. Looking for Exchange 2016 and 2019 information? Tough. Microsoft stated: "Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 are no longer tested for vulnerabilities and there are no updates released. If you are using those versions of Exchange, you should consider them permanently vulnerable [Microsoft's emphasis] and should upgrade your organization immediately." You have been warned.

items.title: Hijacked email accounts complicate investigations into European bomb hoaxes
items.summary: Bomb threats sent to thousands of schools across Europe this week came from a compromised email account at a Taiwanese university, the latest in a series of hoax threats that have targeted airports and newsrooms using messages sent from legitimate institutions. Taiwan’s Da-Yeh University said it suspended the account used on Wednesday to send the emails, according to Taiwan’s Central News Agency. Officials in the Colombian capital Bogotá said last week they were investigating a potential hack impacting a city health agency where other hoax emails originated. The use of hijacked accounts at real and relatively trustworthy institutions has enabled the hoaxers to send messages that pass authentication checks and avoid triggering spam filters. It also introduces challenges for investigators attempting to find out who was responsible. No government has attributed the hoaxes to a specific actor, although the Irish government said last week “it seems likely that this is a coordinated campaign of disruption.” Proofpoint said that while aspects of the campaign “could be consistent with a nation-state-aligned actor,” it did not have enough evidence to reach that conclusion. The email security company Abnormal Security told Recorded Future News it detected another hoax threat sent from what appeared to be “a legitimate, compromised account rather than a spoofed address” on a Lithuanian domain.

items.title: Researcher Drops More Zero-Day Exploits for N-Able Software
items.summary: The researcher who sent managed security providers scrambling globally earlier this week by publishing an exploit chain for N-able software decided Wednesday to pile onto the turmoil by releasing two new exploit chains. Bales said in a LinkedIn post that 4EverAble2Shell "will one-shot a N-central server, and provides root, anonymously," using a remote code execution flaw that can be exploited without having to authenticate. Agent2Shell is a collection of more than 10 zero-day exploits designed "to interact with Windows agents connected to N-central," and which enables remote code execution on the Windows devices with the system level permissions used by the operating system and services, "with the caveat that you know the appliance ID" for the endpoint, he said. In response, N-able at 07:00 UTC on Thursday said that it's investigating the "active incident," quickly took its hosted software online, triggering a "major outage," but also said that its cloud-hosted versions do not appear to be at risk. "Based on our initial review, the server issue described depends on a non-default configuration in which the legacy API is turned on and exposed to the public internet. Legacy API is turned off by default in the product and is not recommended," it said. The company advised: "If legacy API is enabled: disable legacy API now. All other customers: confirm that legacy API is disabled."
